before.heading: Screen every pregnancy
before.body: Test HBsAg during each pregnancy and obtain HBV DNA for an HBsAg-positive patient. Link the parent to liver care and the perinatal prevention program.

after.heading: Screen every pregnancy
after.body: Screen for HBsAg during every pregnancy, preferably in the first trimester, regardless of prior vaccination or testing. If HBsAg is positive, obtain quantitative HBV DNA and assess ALT, HBeAg and maternal liver disease with the treating team. Distinguish treatment needed for maternal health from temporary prophylaxis to reduce transmission. Refer to the Perinatal Hepatitis B Prevention Program and send the original positive laboratory report to the delivery facility and infant clinician. A documented handoff matters even when maternal HBV DNA becomes suppressed.

before.heading: Use maternal prophylaxis when indicated
before.body: Current AASLD guidance supports TDF or selected TAF beginning around week 28 for high viral load under specialist care. WHO guidance also expands prophylaxis eligibility in some settings.

after.heading: Use maternal prophylaxis when indicated
after.body: The 2025 AASLD/IDSA guideline recommends TDF or TAF at gestational week 28 when HBV DNA exceeds 200,000 IU/mL at any time during pregnancy, regardless of HBeAg. TDF has the more extensive pregnancy safety record. If an eligible patient presents after week 28, initiate prophylaxis promptly rather than treating the usual start week as a missed deadline. Continue established TDF/TAF treatment; a patient taking entecavir or another HBV antiviral needs a specialist-directed switch to TDF or TAF. Kidney function, HIV status, other medicines and maternal liver disease still affect the coordinated regimen.

before.heading: Protect the newborn immediately
before.body: An infant born to an HBsAg-positive parent needs vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours. Unknown status requires urgent vaccine and status-directed HBIG action.

after.heading: Protect the newborn immediately
after.body: In the CDC pathway, an infant born to an HBsAg-positive parent needs single-antigen hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) in separate limbs within 12 hours of birth, regardless of birth weight or maternal antiviral use. Vaccine provides active immunity; HBIG provides immediate passive protection. Maternal viral suppression does not replace either newborn intervention. Record both products and administration times, and communicate receipt when the infant transfers to another facility. A missed HBIG dose requires urgent action; the CDC tipsheet permits administration up to seven days after birth, with benefit unlikely beyond that window. Continue vaccination and follow-up even if HBIG was missed.

before.heading: Prove protection
before.body: Complete the vaccine series and obtain post-vaccination serologic testing at the recommended age. Document the result and revaccination or infection pathway if protection failed.

after.heading: Prove protection
after.body: For infants whose parent is HBsAg-positive or whose status remains unknown, complete post-vaccination serologic testing (PVST) with HBsAg and quantitative anti-HBs only at age 9-12 months, or 1-2 months after the final vaccine dose if the series is delayed; do not test before nine months. Earlier testing can detect passive anti-HBs from HBIG or miss late infection. Do not order infant anti-HBc for PVST because maternal antibody may persist up to 24 months. Testing immediately after vaccination can also produce transient HBsAg positivity. Schedule the visit, track the result and report it to the perinatal prevention program.

before.question: What does an infant born to an HBsAg-positive parent need within 12 hours?
choices: Hepatitis B vaccine plus HBIG
Oral entecavir only
No intervention if asymptomatic
Anti-HBs testing before prophylaxis
before.rationale: Immediate active and passive immunoprophylaxis prevents perinatal infection.

after.question: What does an infant born to an HBsAg-positive parent need within 12 hours?
choices: Single-antigen hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG in separate limbs
Single-antigen hepatitis B vaccine alone because HBIG can always wait until the routine visit
HBIG alone, followed by vaccination only if the infant develops symptoms
HBsAg and anti-HBs testing before deciding whether to give prophylaxis
after.rationale: An infant born to an HBsAg-positive parent requires vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours, regardless of birth weight or maternal antiviral use. They provide active and passive protection. Vaccine-only or HBIG-only plans omit part of recommended prophylaxis; waiting for symptoms or serology loses the prevention window. PVST belongs after the completed vaccine series at the recommended age.

before.summary: Maternal viral suppression and newborn immunoprophylaxis are complementary, not competing strategies.
before.application: Create a dated maternal and infant pathway beginning in pregnancy and ending with post-vaccination serology.
keyPoints: Maternal therapy reduces but does not replace infant protection.

after.summary: Coordinate maternal screening and indicated tenofovir with a documented newborn prophylaxis, vaccine-series and serologic follow-up plan. Maternal and infant interventions serve different purposes.
after.application: Build a dated plan from prenatal screening through postpartum maternal monitoring and infant PVST. State maternal treatment purpose, delivery status and birth weight, product timing, series completion, result interpretation and follow-up ownership.
keyPoints: Screen HBsAg during every pregnancy and assess HBV DNA when positive.
AASLD and WHO use distinct prophylaxis thresholds and timing.
Positive maternal HBsAg requires infant vaccine plus HBIG within 12 hours regardless of weight.
Unknown maternal status requires an urgent test and a birth-weight-specific infant plan.
PVST uses HBsAg and anti-HBs at the correct age; omit infant anti-HBc.
A postpartum antiviral stop needs maternal eligibility review and monitored follow-up.

pregnancy-infant.heading: Keep the WHO pathway distinct
pregnancy-infant.body: WHO recommendations retained in the 2026 handbook use TDF for HBsAg-positive pregnancy with HBV DNA at least 200,000 IU/mL or positive HBeAg, preferably from the second trimester until at least delivery or completion of the infant vaccine series. When neither HBV DNA nor HBeAg testing is available, WHO conditionally recommends TDF for all HBsAg-positive pregnant patients; this has low-certainty evidence. Assess long-term maternal treatment eligibility without delaying prophylaxis. WHO pairs maternal prophylaxis with a timely infant vaccine birth dose, preferably within 24 hours, and at least three total vaccine doses. Apply the national pathway rather than mixing its timing with the U.S. CDC exposed-infant 12-hour plan.

pregnancy-infant.heading: Plan postpartum care before delivery
pregnancy-infant.body: AASLD allows TDF/TAF to stop at delivery when the sole indication is perinatal prophylaxis and there is no continuing maternal treatment need. Cirrhosis or another ongoing indication requires continued therapy. After a planned stop, monitor HBV DNA and ALT every 1-3 months for up to six months; AASLD directs treatment reinitiation for a significant withdrawal flare, defined here as ALT at least five times the upper limit of normal. Arrange responsibility for results and urgent assessment of worsening disease. AASLD supports TDF or TAF during breastfeeding. Earlier prophylaxis may be appropriate with preterm-labor risk or anticipated invasive procedures; if infant HBIG is unavailable, AASLD advises starting at week 16 in high-viremia pregnancy with subsequent infant vaccination. This access-dependent pathway requires expert coordination.

pregnancy-infant.heading: Resolve unknown maternal status
pregnancy-infant.body: If maternal HBsAg documentation is unavailable at delivery, draw and test it urgently. With no other evidence of maternal HBV infection, a newborn weighing at least 2,000 g needs single-antigen vaccine within 12 hours while the result is pending; if the parent tests positive, give HBIG as soon as possible and no later than seven days of age. Below 2,000 g, give vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours when status is unknown. If maternal HBV DNA, positive HBeAg or known chronic HBV already indicates infection, treat the infant as exposed to an HBsAg-positive parent regardless of a missing HBsAg report. If status remains unknown, retain the exposed-infant series and PVST plan.

pregnancy-infant.heading: Complete the birth-weight-specific series
pregnancy-infant.body: For an exposed infant weighing at least 2,000 g, the CDC single-antigen schedule is birth, 1-2 months and six months; an appropriate combination-vaccine schedule after the single-antigen birth dose may produce four total doses. Below 2,000 g with positive or unknown maternal status, the birth dose does not count toward the primary series: give three additional doses beginning at one month, for four total doses. The final dose has a minimum age of 24 weeks; observe the product schedule and minimum intervals. For a documented HBsAg-negative parent, the currently posted CDC schedule gives medically stable infants at least 2,000 g vaccine within 24 hours; below 2,000 g, give the first dose at one month or hospital discharge, whichever is earlier. These negative-status rules do not justify delaying prophylaxis in an exposed infant.

pregnancy-infant.heading: Act on the PVST result
pregnancy-infant.body: After a documented complete series, HBsAg-negative infants with anti-HBs at least 10 mIU/mL are protected and need no additional HBV vaccine follow-up. If HBsAg is negative and anti-HBs is below 10 mIU/mL, ACIP recommends one additional vaccine dose and repeat PVST 1-2 months later. If anti-HBs remains below 10, give two more doses to complete the second series and retest 1-2 months after its final dose. A complete second three-dose series followed by retesting is an alternative based on clinical circumstances or family preference. Further doses have no demonstrated benefit after two complete series without response. HBsAg positivity requires infection follow-up, not a routine nonresponse vaccination pathway.

Finaldoseminimum24weeks, negative-parent >=2000g medicallystable24h vs<2000g1month/discharge earlier accurate. 164days figure is4daygrace, not24x7 arithmetic.

wholeBody.heading: Act on the PVST result
wholeBody.body: After a documented complete series, HBsAg-negative infants with anti-HBs at least 10 mIU/mL are protected and need no additional HBV vaccine follow-up. If HBsAg is negative and anti-HBs is below 10 mIU/mL, ACIP recommends one additional vaccine dose and repeat PVST 1-2 months later. If anti-HBs remains below 10, give two more doses to complete the second series and retest 1-2 months after its final dose. A complete second three-dose series followed by retesting is an alternative based on clinical circumstances or family preference. Further doses have no demonstrated benefit after two complete series without response. HBsAg positivity requires infection follow-up, not a routine nonresponse vaccination pathway.

wholeBodyComparisons.comparison: HBsAg-negative/antiHBs>=10 protected inclusive exact10; <10 single-dose/retest1-2m then2additional/retest1-2m second-series path; full3dosealternative andtwo-series limit preserved. HBsAgpositive refersforinfection, notroutineantibody-onlyrevax.

wholeQuestion.question: Which statement is most accurate? Focus: pregnancy.
choices: AASLD recommends TDF or TAF at week 28 for HBV DNA above 200,000 IU/mL; TDF has more pregnancy safety experience
AASLD requires positive HBeAg as well as HBV DNA above 200,000 IU/mL for perinatal prophylaxis
AASLD considers entecavir the preferred perinatal prophylaxis regardless of existing therapy
Successful maternal prophylaxis replaces the infant vaccine and HBIG plan
wholeQuestion.rationale: The 2025 AASLD recommendation uses HBV DNA above 200,000 IU/mL at any time in pregnancy regardless of HBeAg. It supports TDF or TAF at week 28 and recognizes more extensive TDF pregnancy safety experience. Entecavir requires a pregnancy-appropriate specialist switch, and maternal treatment never removes the exposed infant CDC prophylaxis requirement.

wholeQuestionComparisons.singleBestAnswerComparison: Only threshold-basedTDF/TAFstatement correct. HBeAgextraAND,preferredETV andmaternal-replaces-infant claims false.

wholeQuestion.question: Which action best applies the evidence? Focus: pregnancy.
choices: At week 31 with HBV DNA 350,000 IU/mL, arrange prompt TDF or TAF prophylaxis and the infant vaccine/HBIG plan
At week 31 with HBV DNA 350,000 IU/mL, withhold prophylaxis because the week-28 start has passed
At week 31 with HBV DNA 350,000 IU/mL, give the mother HBIG instead of considering antiviral prophylaxis
At week 31 with HBV DNA 350,000 IU/mL, use a single maternal vaccine dose to suppress established HBV
wholeQuestion.rationale: HBV DNA 350,000 IU/mL exceeds the AASLD prophylaxis threshold. Its implementation guidance directs initiation promptly when an eligible patient presents after week 28. Maternal HBIG or vaccine does not substitute for antiviral suppression of established infection, and newborn vaccine plus HBIG is still required when maternal HBsAg is positive.

wholeQuestionComparisons.singleBestAnswerComparison: 31week350000eligiblelate-presentation immediateinitiationwithinfantplan unique best. Missedweekdeadline, maternalHBIGsubstitution andvaccinesuppressestablishedinfection wrong.

wholeQuestion.question: Which plan demonstrates the strongest clinical reasoning? Focus: pregnancy.
choices: Before stopping at delivery, distinguish temporary prophylaxis from ongoing maternal treatment; continue indicated therapy and arrange monitored follow-up if a stop is appropriate
Stop every HBV antiviral at delivery, including treatment for cirrhosis, because perinatal transmission risk ends at birth
After a prophylaxis-only stop, use infant anti-HBs instead of maternal HBV DNA and ALT to assess withdrawal flares
Prohibit breastfeeding for every patient taking TDF or TAF, even when infant prophylaxis has been completed
wholeQuestion.rationale: AASLD permits a delivery-time stop only when prophylaxis was the sole indication and maternal therapy is not otherwise needed. A planned stop requires HBV DNA and ALT monitoring every 1-3 months for up to six months. Infant antibody does not measure maternal flares. AASLD supports TDF or TAF during breastfeeding; ongoing maternal treatment needs remain relevant.

wholeQuestionComparisons.singleBestAnswerComparison: Maternalindicationreview/appropriatecontinuation orplannedstopwithmonitoring unique best. Automaticstopincirrhosis, infantantiHBs maternalflareproxy andabsoluteTDF/TAFbreastfeedban incorrect.

wholeQuestion.question: Which error creates the greatest avoidable risk? Focus: pregnancy.
choices: Stop indicated HBV therapy at delivery in a patient with cirrhosis and arrange no maternal follow-up
Check whether a pregnant patient taking entecavir needs a specialist-directed switch to TDF or TAF
Screen HBsAg in the current pregnancy even when a previous pregnancy had a negative result
Coordinate the maternal antiviral plan with the delivery facility and infant clinician
wholeQuestion.rationale: The avoidable-risk action is stopping treatment needed for maternal cirrhosis and omitting follow-up. Delivery does not eliminate maternal HBV treatment needs or withdrawal-flare risk. Pregnancy-appropriate regimen review, current-pregnancy screening and a documented delivery handoff are protective actions.

wholeQuestionComparisons.singleBestAnswerComparison: Key now actualharmfulstopincirrhosis withoutfollowup. Allothers protective actions; no competingbest.

wholeQuestion.question: Which statement is most accurate? Focus: infant prophylaxis.
choices: An infant of an HBsAg-positive parent needs single-antigen vaccine and HBIG in separate limbs within 12 hours regardless of birth weight
An infant of an HBsAg-positive parent can omit HBIG when maternal HBV DNA becomes undetectable
An infant below 2,000 g with an HBsAg-positive parent should wait until one month for all prophylaxis
An infant of an HBsAg-positive parent needs anti-HBc testing at birth before vaccine or HBIG
wholeQuestion.rationale: CDC recommends both active vaccine and passive HBIG protection within 12 hours for all infants of HBsAg-positive parents. Maternal suppression and low birth weight do not remove that requirement. The low-weight birth dose is followed by three additional vaccine doses. Anti-HBc is not part of infant PVST and should not delay prophylaxis.

wholeQuestion.question: Which action best applies the evidence? Focus: infant prophylaxis.
choices: For a 2,300-g newborn with maternal HBsAg pending and no other evidence of maternal HBV, give vaccine within 12 hours, test urgently and give HBIG promptly if positive, no later than day seven
For a 2,300-g newborn with maternal HBsAg pending and no other evidence of maternal HBV, wait for the result before giving any vaccine
For a 2,300-g newborn with maternal HBsAg pending and no other evidence of maternal HBV, give vaccine at birth but never add HBIG if the result later becomes positive
For a 2,300-g newborn with maternal HBsAg pending and no other evidence of maternal HBV, use the one-month vaccine delay allowed for a small infant of a negative parent
wholeQuestion.rationale: At least 2,000 g with unknown maternal status and no other infection evidence, vaccine is due within 12 hours while testing proceeds. A positive result triggers HBIG as soon as possible and no later than seven days. The negative-parent low-weight delay does not fit this case. Below 2,000 g with unknown status, CDC requires vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours.

wholeQuestionComparisons.singleBestAnswerComparison: 2300g/nootherHBVevidence pending-status12hvaccinewithurgenttest/positiveHBIGby7d uniquebest. Neitherresultwaiting, neveraddingHBIG nornegative-parent-lowweight rule appropriate.

wholeQuestion.question: Which plan demonstrates the strongest clinical reasoning? Focus: infant prophylaxis.
choices: For an exposed infant at ten months after a complete series, HBsAg-negative with anti-HBs 8 mIU/mL, give one additional vaccine dose and repeat PVST in 1-2 months
For an exposed infant at ten months after a complete series, HBsAg-negative with anti-HBs 8 mIU/mL, declare protection because any detectable antibody is sufficient
For an exposed infant at ten months after a complete series, HBsAg-negative with anti-HBs 8 mIU/mL, diagnose active infection from the low antibody alone
For an exposed infant at ten months after a complete series, HBsAg-negative with anti-HBs 8 mIU/mL, order anti-HBc instead of arranging revaccination
wholeQuestion.rationale: The protected infant pattern requires negative HBsAg and anti-HBs at least 10 mIU/mL after a documented series. At 8 mIU/mL with negative HBsAg, ACIP recommends one additional dose and retesting in 1-2 months; persistent low anti-HBs leads to two further doses and another test. Low anti-HBs alone does not establish infection, and maternal anti-HBc can persist in infancy.

wholeQuestionComparisons.singleBestAnswerComparison: 10month completed-seriesnegativeHBsAgantiHBs8 needs additionaldose/retest. Any-antibody protection, low-antibody-only infectiondiagnosis andantiHBcsubstitution incorrect.

wholeQuestion.question: Which error creates the greatest avoidable risk? Focus: infant prophylaxis.
choices: Delay all prophylaxis until one month in a 1,800-g infant of an HBsAg-positive parent, applying the negative-parent low-weight rule
Give that exposed low-weight infant vaccine and HBIG in separate limbs within 12 hours
Plan three additional vaccine doses beginning at one month for that exposed low-weight infant
Arrange HBsAg and anti-HBs PVST at age 9-12 months after completing that infant vaccine series
wholeQuestion.rationale: Delaying all prophylaxis exposes this infant to avoidable transmission risk. The one-month or discharge delay applies to an infant below 2,000 g with a documented HBsAg-negative parent. Positive maternal HBsAg requires vaccine plus HBIG within 12 hours regardless of weight, followed by three additional doses and appropriately timed PVST.

wholeQuestionComparisons.singleBestAnswerComparison: Actualharmfulaction is delayallprophin1800gpositive-parentinfant. Threeotherchoices positive-status12hproph,3additionaldoses and9-12moPVST appropriate.

wholeLesson.title: Break Perinatal Transmission
wholeLesson.summary: Coordinate maternal screening and indicated tenofovir with a documented newborn prophylaxis, vaccine-series and serologic follow-up plan. Maternal and infant interventions serve different purposes.
wholeLesson.application: Build a dated plan from prenatal screening through postpartum maternal monitoring and infant PVST. State maternal treatment purpose, delivery status and birth weight, product timing, series completion, result interpretation and follow-up ownership.
keyPoints: Screen HBsAg during every pregnancy and assess HBV DNA when positive.
AASLD and WHO use distinct prophylaxis thresholds and timing.
Positive maternal HBsAg requires infant vaccine plus HBIG within 12 hours regardless of weight.
Unknown maternal status requires an urgent test and a birth-weight-specific infant plan.
PVST uses HBsAg and anti-HBs at the correct age; omit infant anti-HBc.
A postpartum antiviral stop needs maternal eligibility review and monitored follow-up.

check.question: What does an infant born to an HBsAg-positive parent need within 12 hours?
choices: Single-antigen hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG in separate limbs
Single-antigen hepatitis B vaccine alone because HBIG can always wait until the routine visit
HBIG alone, followed by vaccination only if the infant develops symptoms
HBsAg and anti-HBs testing before deciding whether to give prophylaxis
check.rationale: An infant born to an HBsAg-positive parent requires vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours, regardless of birth weight or maternal antiviral use. They provide active and passive protection. Vaccine-only or HBIG-only plans omit part of recommended prophylaxis; waiting for symptoms or serology loses the prevention window. PVST belongs after the completed vaccine series at the recommended age.
